items.title: James Lincoln Collier interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007
items.q: I was Don’s upper class advisor... we put him up... we fought... to get the majority

ctx.x: No, this would have been later, after I was maybe a junior or something, ‘48, somewhere around in there. But during that time I and three or four or five or six other members of my house, because there were no blacks in any fraternity and hardly any blacks on the campus mind you, but there were no blacks in any fraternity. And we said, this group of us said, we’re going to do something about this. And so there was a young freshman called Don Thomas and last I heard he was living in New York on the Upper West…

saying ELS is going to take care of the blacks, and so we had a moral crisis over every black kid that was admitted to Hamilton after that. But I think it helped the administration to see that the students were not going to have a problem with this, they just weren’t. And so then of course things began to change and the situation began to open up and obviously improve. But I wanted that on record.
